title: Emergent Non-Markovian Nonlinear Qubit From Collective Spin Interactions
authors: Gregory T. Carroll, Michael R. Geller, Andre Erpenbeck
abstract: Open-system descriptions are typically introduced by coupling a quantum system to an external environment. Here we show that a closed interacting many-body system can itself generate a controlled non-Markovian quantum channel acting on a reduced nonlinear qubit through finite-size corrections to a nonlinear mean-field limit. We demonstrate this using the Kitagawa-Ueda one-axis twisting model, $H=χJ_z^2$, a paradigmatic model of collective spin dynamics, spin squeezing, and two-component Bose-Einstein condensates. Although the large-$N$ regime of this model has been extensively studied, the conventional fixed-$χ$ scaling does not yield a nontrivial dynamical large-$N$ limit. In this paper, we investigate a complementary large-$N$ formulation obtained from the double limit $N\rightarrow\infty$ and $χ\rightarrow O(g/N)$, where $g$ is a coupling constant. We derive the leading finite-$N$ corrections to this limit and show that they correspond to an emergent non-Markovian dephasing process, producing a Gaussian decay of the Bloch-vector coherence with characteristic timescale $t_\varphi\geq\sqrt{N}/(2g)$. Exact finite-$N$ calculations demonstrate that this effective open-system description becomes quantitatively accurate for systems containing on the order of one hundred qubits. The resulting framework provides a microscopic realization of non-Markovian dephasing generated intrinsically by a closed many-body system and enables efficient simulation of collective quantum dynamics beyond unitary mean-field theory. These results link the long-studied phenomenon of phase diffusion in atomic ensembles and Bose-Einstein condensates to the growing effort to characterize non-Markovian, beyond-Lindblad noise in quantum computing hardware, providing a rare case in which such a noise channel is derived from microscopic dynamics rather than fit phenomenologically.
summary: The paper demonstrates that collective spin interactions within a closed many-body system can effectively mimic coupling to an environment, generating non-Markovian dephasing. By analyzing finite-size corrections to the mean-field limit, the authors derive an effective open-system description for the reduced qubit dynamics. This provides a powerful theoretical tool linking fundamental quantum dynamics to noise characterization in quantum information.
main_problem: The study investigates how an effective non-Markovian quantum channel can emerge intrinsically from a closed, interacting many-body system, bypassing the need for explicit environmental coupling.
main_result: Finite-size corrections to the large-$N$ mean-field limit of the collective spin model generate an emergent non-Markovian dephasing process characterized by Gaussian coherence decay with a timescale proportional to $\sqrt{N}$.
method: The authors derive this effect by analyzing the double large-$N$ limit ($\chi = g/N$) and calculating the leading finite-$N$ corrections using Maclaurin series expansions of time-evolution functions.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using the Kitagawa-Ueda one-axis twisting model, $H=\chi J_z^2$, which describes collective spin dynamics. The analysis reduces the complex many-body problem to an effective nonlinear qubit description.
key_observables: Bloch vector coherence decay (Gaussian form), magnetization $\langle\vec{J}angle$, and the characteristic dephasing timescale $t_\phi$.
important_parameters: The system size $N$ is crucial, as the non-Markovian effects become apparent in finite-$N$ corrections; the scaling limit involves $\chi \propto 1/N$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the leading finite-$N$ corrections can be accurately captured by a Maclaurin series expansion of the time evolution function.
figures_summary: Figures compare exact finite-$N$ simulations against large-$N$ approximations, demonstrating the emergence of non-Markovian decay and showing that pure dephasing successfully models the dynamics better than isotropic depolarization.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (KU Hamiltonian), identifies the necessary scaling limit ($\chi=g/N$), derives the leading finite-$N$ corrections to the mean-field theory, and then validates this resulting non-Markovian dephasing channel against exact numerical simulations.
why_interesting: This work provides a rare microscopic derivation of non-Markovian noise—a key challenge in quantum computing hardware characterization—directly from the Hamiltonian dynamics of an isolated system.
